rules: The 15 October 20 provisional new groups cannot be counted as 15 additional customs: 11 have current canonical IDs, four remain provisional P2.
A 54-card editorial draft is a source-derived editorial candidate, not necessarily a distinct custom.
Regional reference, other-owner content, and ministerial rite holds remain retained, not automatically inserted into the Customs catalogue.
The 14 same-practice grouping suggestions are reversible and do not merge records. Related variant families are conceptual linkages only.

historical_uncertainties: Exact first origin and path of diffusion remain disputed.
Specific local prayers, routes and host practices vary; no one form should be called universal.
Older-origin claims need archival corroboration; avoid a precise century.
Related wafers in Lithuania, Slovakia and elsewhere should retain their own names and local details.
Exact chronology between Rome's seven-basilica pilgrimage and dispersed Holy Thursday altar visits varies among accounts.
No indulgence, prescribed set of prayers or seven-visit obligation is asserted.
Chronology and first Catholic domestic use differ among secondary summaries; 1925 Cologne refers to a Catholic church wreath, not the first household wreath.
Independent historical evidence for this exact domestic form is limited; retain 'optional contemporary adaptation'.
Do not supply a lay ritual, field-sprinkling formula or claim that a priestly blessing is available.
French origin and antiquity remain unverified independently; label as a modern family-reported custom, not a proven French historical tradition.
Do not conflate the Polish hay-under-table custom with the manger-straw practice.
Exact medieval origins and continuity vary by locality; the secure, documented Austrian charitable revival begins in 1954.
Direct descent from Roman Saturnalia is unproven; keep only as a commonly repeated theory if mentioned.
The extra poor-person's share is historically attested in some accounts but not universal today.
A 1962 feast date and a modern French Sunday celebration should not be conflated.
The precise earliest origin is unclear for these crafts and differs by place.
Arbúcies' current secular festival is not identical to the earlier procession custom.
Local feast/procession transfer must be verified; calendar date alone does not establish an event.
Exact historical beginnings of the modern walk are not established by these sources.
Weiser's French/Canadian grandparent-visiting variant is not verified by these witnesses and must not be folded into the German/Austrian practice.
Do not project the 1930s–1950s named Mary Garden movement into medieval history.
Plant legends vary and should never be asserted as fact without separate historical evidence.
